title: Comprehensive Mirror for Aid in Government
subtitle: Reflecting on Past Events · Aiding the Way of Governance · A Mirror for a Thousand Years
description: "Comprehensive Mirror for Aid in Government" (Zizhi Tongjian), compiled under the direction of Sima Guang of the Northern Song dynasty over nineteen years, comprises 294 chapters and over three million characters. It spans from the twenty-third year of King Weilie of Zhou (403 BC) to the sixth year of the Xiande reign of Emperor Shizong of Later Zhou (959 AD), encompassing 1,362 years of history. Emperor Shenzong of Song bestowed the title "Comprehensive Mirror for Aid in Government"—meaning "reflecting on past events to aid the way of governance." It is the greatest chronological history in Chinese history, standing together with the "Records of the Grand Historian" as the "twin jades of historiography."

route.title: Journey Through the Comprehensive Mirror: A Tour of Millennial Governance Through National Treasures
route.intro:
Reflecting on the rise and fall of former ages, examine the gains and losses of the present.
Sima Guang (1019–1086), courtesy name Junshi, was a native of Xia County, Shanzhou (present-day Xia County, Shanxi). His childhood story of smashing a vat to rescue a friend is well known. Less known is that he spent nineteen years organizing the compilation of this three-million-character magnum opus. During Wang Anshi's reforms, Sima Guang retired to Luoyang, burying himself in historical research at his Garden of Solitary Joy. He consulted over three hundred types of historical sources—standard histories, unofficial accounts, court records, genealogies, tomb inscriptions—examining and reconciling differences item by item. He first compiled the "Textual Criticism of the Comprehensive Mirror" before finalizing the draft—this rigorous method of source criticism was unprecedented. Wang Fuzhi's "Reading the Comprehensive Mirror" evaluated the work: "Profound indeed is Sima Guang's naming of this compilation. By 'aid in government,' he means not merely knowing order and disorder, but providing the means for vigorously seeking good governance." The "Comprehensive Mirror for Aid in Government" was not meant for idle reading—it is a mirror, reflecting the successes and failures of all dynasties, showing later generations what to do and what not to do. Let us follow the timeline of the "Comprehensive Mirror," traversing the historical corridor from the Warring States to the Five Dynasties, visiting six sites of nationally protected cultural relics that bear witness to millennial cycles of order and chaos.

stops.title: Stop One: The Ancient City of Zheng and Han in Xinzheng: The Partition of Jin, Where the Comprehensive Mirror Begins
stops.content: The opening of the "Comprehensive Mirror for Aid in Government" is carefully crafted. Most histories begin with high antiquity, but Sima Guang chose to start from the twenty-third year of King Weilie of Zhou (403 BC)—the year the Zhou Son of Heaven formally recognized Han, Zhao, and Wei as feudal lords. In the opening passage, Sima Guang wrote his famous "Your servant Guang says": "Your servant has heard that the duty of the Son of Heaven is nothing greater than upholding ritual. Ritual is nothing greater than maintaining the social hierarchy. Social hierarchy is nothing greater than preserving the proper names. What is ritual? It is the guiding principles. What is social hierarchy? It is ruler and subject. What are proper names? They are duke, marquis, high minister, and grand master." He pointed out that the partition of Jin was a watershed not because the State of Jin was carved up—but because the Zhou Son of Heaven actually acknowledged this usurpation! The collapse of rites and music began from this moment. The Ancient City of Zheng and Han (Including Han King Mausoleums) was the later capital of the State of Han. In the partition of Jin, Han received a small slice of territory in the heart of the warring states, making it the weakest of the Seven Powers. Yet Han's iron-smelting technology was unmatched in the realm: "The swords and halberds of Han's soldiers... cut through oxen and horses on land and pierce swans and geese in the water." But technological superiority could not overcome geographical disadvantage—Han was the first of the six states to fall to Qin. The ancient city of Zheng and Han spans over four hundred years of two states. Its walls measure about forty li in circumference, forming an irregular rectangle. The city is divided into eastern and western sections: the western city housed the palace and administrative area, the eastern city contained workshops and residential quarters. Archaeological excavations have yielded large quantities of Warring States bronze ritual vessels, iron tools, and weapons. The iron-smelting workshop sites alone have produced thousands of iron objects—confirming the "Records of the Grand Historian" passage that "the swords and halberds of Han's soldiers all come from Mingshan and Tangxi." Most astonishingly, Han swordsmiths had mastered the "composite sword" technique—the blade and spine were cast separately using bronze with different tin contents, then joined into one, giving a sharp edge and a tough spine. Standing on the city wall, looking at the broken bricks and tiles, you stand at the very historical node that opens the first page of the "Comprehensive Mirror"—the Son of Heaven's authority, here reduced to piles of silent rammed earth.

stops.title: Stop Two: The Great Wall: Qin Conquered the Realm by Force, and Fell in Two Generations
stops.content: The "Comprehensive Mirror's" account of the rise and fall of the Qin dynasty is powerfully narrated. In the twenty-sixth year of the First Emperor (221 BC), "The King had just united the realm, considering his virtue to surpass that of the Three Sovereigns and his achievements to exceed those of the Five Emperors, so he changed his title to Emperor." Yet just fifteen years later, the vast empire collapsed like a house of cards. Sima Guang recorded in vivid detail the First Emperor's construction of the Great Wall, the imperial highways, the Epang Palace, and the Lishan Mausoleum, as well as the burning of books and burying of scholars. He also recorded Chen Sheng and Wu Guang's cry: "Are kings and generals, ministers and chancellors, born to their stations?" The Great Wall, this dragon stretching across northern China, occupies a special place in the "Comprehensive Mirror." Meng Tian led 300,000 troops north to drive out the Xiongnu, "taking advantage of the terrain to establish strategic passes, from Lintao to Liaodong, extending over 10,000 li." But at the end of the Qin Annals, Sima Guang quoted Jia Yi's "Discourse on the Faults of Qin" with piercing insight: "Benevolence and righteousness were not practiced, so the balance between offensive and defensive power shifted." Building the Great Wall was not itself wrong—every dynasty built it—but the First Emperor's problem was that he thought the Wall would ensure his security, unaware that the true wall is the people's hearts. Sima Guang also recorded a detail in the "Comprehensive Mirror": the First Emperor built imperial highways, "fifty paces wide, with trees planted every three zhang"—these were ancient superhighways, the central lane reserved for the Son of Heaven, flanked by green pines marking the distance. Yet like the Great Wall, these highways were built on the backs of harsh conscript labor. Taxes and corvee labor "thirty times those of antiquity" made the people's lives unbearable. Chen Sheng and Wu Guang rose up at Dazexiang because they were caught in the rain on their way to garrison Yuyang and delayed—under Qin law, "those who miss the deadline are executed." A single shout of defiance began the fall of Qin. At the end of the "Comprehensive Mirror—Qin Annals," Jia Yi's words are quoted: "The lessons of the past not forgotten serve as teachers for the future." Standing at the foot of the Great Wall, looking up at this vast engineering marvel, you cannot help but ask: how could a dynasty that built the Great Wall be overthrown by a group of conscripts? Sima Guang engraved the answer in every character: governance does not depend on the height of walls, but on where the people's hearts lie. Today, standing on the Great Wall, watching the dragon wind over the mountaintops, you understand Sima Guang's profound meaning: defensive works built of brick and stone will eventually crumble; only virtuous governance is a wall that can never be broken.

stops.title: Stop Three: Maoling: The Martial Spirit of Emperor Wu of Han and His Edict of Repentance at Luntai
stops.content: Sima Guang's attitude toward Emperor Wu of Han is profoundly complex. The "Comprehensive Mirror—Han Annals" records in detail Liu Che's brilliant military campaigns: Wei Qing's seven expeditions deep into the northern deserts, Huo Qubing's "Until the Xiongnu are destroyed, I will not marry," Zhang Qian's pioneering of the Western Regions. Yet it also frankly exposes Emperor Wu's failures in his later years: exhausting the nation's resources through incessant warfare, "the realm drained, the population halved"; his superstition, seeking immortality from alchemists, resulting in a series of absurdities; the Witchcraft Scandal, in which Crown Prince Ju was forced to rebel and Chang'an ran with blood. The sealed earth of the Maoling Mausoleum rises majestically; the stone carving of "The Horse Trampling a Xiongnu" before the mausoleum proclaims the might of the Han empire. Yet what Sima Guang treasured more was the "Edict of Repentance Issued from Luntai" that Emperor Wu proclaimed two years before his death—"Since I ascended the throne, I have acted wildly and perversely, causing distress throughout the realm. I cannot undo the past. From now on, all matters that harm the people and waste the nation's resources shall be abolished!" For a suspicious, autocratic ruler to publicly acknowledge his mistakes in his old age—what extraordinary rarity! Sima Guang quoted this edict in full in the "Comprehensive Mirror"—because he knew that a ruler who can "blame himself" is a truly great ruler. Standing before Maoling, thinking back to that ambitious young emperor who ascended the throne at sixteen, now lying alone beneath the earth at sixty-nine—what the "Comprehensive Mirror for Aid in Government" teaches us is not to praise power, but to guard against its corrosive influence.

stops.title: Stop Four: Longmen Grottoes and Shaolin Temple: Flickers of Faith in a Time of Chaos
stops.content: The Wei-Jin Southern and Northern Dynasties period is the most suffocating stretch in the "Comprehensive Mirror." Sima Guang uses major events such as the Disaster of Yongjia, the Five Barbarian Invasions, and the Rebellion of Hou Jing to chronicle nearly three hundred years of warfare and division. Yet he also records one small but meaningful episode: after Emperor Xiaowen of Northern Wei, Tuoba Hong, moved the capital to Luoyang, he vigorously promoted sinicization reforms—changing Xianbei surnames to Han names, adopting Han dress and language, and ordering the carving of the Longmen Grottoes. The Longmen Grottoes began in the Northern Wei and flourished in the Tang. They now contain 2,345 niches and over 100,000 statues. The Vairocana Buddha at Fengxian Temple stands seventeen meters tall, his serene countenance gazing down at the Yi River for a thousand years. In that age of incessant warfare, people carved their prayers for peace into the stone—these Buddhist images are not cold works of art, but a flicker of light grasped by countless ordinary people in their despair. Equally important is the Shaolin Temple—founded in the nineteenth year of Taihe of Northern Wei (495 AD) for the Indian monk Buddhabhadra. Later, Bodhidharma sat facing a wall for nine years here, founding the Chan School. Sima Guang's account includes the famous dialogue between Bodhidharma and Emperor Wu of Liang—the Emperor asked: "Since I ascended the throne, I have built temples, copied sutras, and ordained monks beyond counting. What merit have I earned?" Bodhidharma replied: "No merit at all." The "Comprehensive Mirror" records this conversation because Sima Guang understood that the true meaning of faith lies not in outward forms but in the heart.

stops.title: Stop Five: The Grand Canal: A Microcosm of the Rise and Fall of the Sui and Tang Dynasties
stops.content: The "Comprehensive Mirror's" critique of Emperor Yang of Sui is among the most vehement in the entire work. Emperor Yang of Sui, Yang Guang, dug the Grand Canal—this great engineering project of 2,700 kilometers connected the five major river systems of north and south China: "From then on, the realm benefited from the transport of goods." But Sima Guang records in painstaking detail the horrific cost of building the canal: millions of conscripts were levied, "four or five out of ten laborers died." When combined with three campaigns against Goguryeo, the construction of the Eastern Capital, and the building of the Great Wall, the Sui dynasty exhausted the people's strength in just thirty-seven years and collapsed in the second generation. The Grand Canal was fully utilized in the Tang dynasty, becoming the economic artery connecting north and south and giving rise to the Kaiyuan Golden Age. Yet after the An Lushan Rebellion, canal transport was intermittently disrupted. The central government lost effective control over the wealth of Jiangnan, and the power of regional military governors grew ever stronger—the fate of a single canal was linked to the rise and fall of the entire empire. Today the Grand Canal is a UNESCO World Heritage site, and cities along its route—Hangzhou, Yangzhou, Suzhou, Luoyang—remain prosperous. Standing on the canal's banks, watching the barges pass, you understand Sima Guang's intent: why were the same large-scale projects—the First Emperor's Great Wall, Emperor Yang's Grand Canal—both "meritorious for a thousand ages but crimes against their own times"? Because they forced the people to labor for their own private glory, rather than "taking the people's hearts as their own hearts." This mirror reflects the conscience of every ruler.

stops.title: Stop Six: The Iron Pagoda in Kaifeng: The Final Chapter of the Five Dynasties' Turmoil
stops.content: The "Comprehensive Mirror" ends in the sixth year of the Xiande reign of Emperor Shizong of Later Zhou (959 AD)—Shizong, Chai Rong, died young, and Zhao Kuangyin's assumption of power through a yellow robe was about to unfold. Sima Guang chose to end here with deep intent: the Five Dynasties and Ten Kingdoms period was one of the most chaotic in Chinese history. In fifty-three years, five dynasties and eight surnames of fourteen emperors rose and fell: "The emperor was whoever had the strongest army." Yet from the ashes of this chaos, the great Song dynasty was about to be born. The Youguo Temple Pagoda (commonly known as the Kaifeng Iron Pagoda) was built in the first year of the Huangyou reign of the Northern Song (1049 AD), not long before the completion of the "Comprehensive Mirror." This thirteen-story glazed brick pagoda stands fifty-five meters high, its brown color giving it an iron-like appearance from a distance. It is the tallest and oldest surviving glazed pagoda in China. It witnessed the most splendid years of the Northern Song—Kaifeng's population exceeded one million, its prosperity unmatched in the world. Sima Guang did not live to see Kaifeng fall, but he must have sensed something was coming. The "Comprehensive Mirror for Aid in Government" was completed in the seventh year of the Yuanfeng reign (1084 AD). Just forty-two years later, the Jingkang Incident occurred, and the Northern Song fell. Yet the historical wisdom embodied in the "Comprehensive Mirror" transcends dynastic changes. It tells every later generation: the way of rise and fall lies not in the Mandate of Heaven but in the hearts of the people. "Reflecting on past events to aid the way of governance"—this is Sima Guang's legacy to all Chinese people.
